analysis.one_liner: Stops apps and data brokers from collecting and selling personal reproductive and sexual health data.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 11, 2025, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote; it has 101 cosponsors, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar companies outside the doctor's-office health system — period-tracking apps, fertility apps, telehealth sites, and data brokers — from collecting, keeping, or sharing personal reproductive or sexual health information unless it is strictly necessary to provide the service the person asked for. It would give people the right to see, correct, and delete that data within 15 days, free of charge, and would let the Federal Trade Commission enforce the rules and let individuals sue violators for $100 to $1,000 per violation per day. It has not moved past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who uses period trackers, fertility apps, telehealth services, pharmacy websites, or maps to find a clinic. The bill would stop that data from being sold to data brokers or used for targeted advertising, and would give users direct control to view, correct, and delete it. The private right of action — with statutory damages and a ban on forced arbitration for these disputes — means a person could sue without proving a dollar amount of harm.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of reproductive and sexual health apps

how_it_helps.text: Bars regulated entities from collecting, retaining, using, or disclosing personal reproductive or sexual health information except as strictly necessary to provide a requested product or service, and restricts which employees can access it.

Covers inferred and algorithmic data as well as location information that might indicate someone is trying to obtain reproductive or sexual health services, not just information a person typed in directly.

Gives individuals enforceable rights to access, correct, and delete their data within 15 days at no fee, including data the company bought from third parties or inferred about them, plus disclosure of exactly which third parties received it.

Lets the FTC enforce violations and lets individuals sue for $100–$1,000 per violation per day or actual damages, whichever is greater, with punitive damages and attorney's fees available; pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers cannot be used to block these suits.
Prohibits companies from retaliating against users who exercise their rights, such as by charging them more or degrading service.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers, advertising-tech companies, and app developers lose a data stream they currently collect, sell, and use for targeted advertising, and they bear the cost of building deletion and access systems. Companies also face litigation exposure from the per-day statutory damages. Small app developers would feel compliance costs most acutely.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad-tech firms, and app developers

drawbacks.text: The private right of action with statutory damages of $100 to $1,000 per violation per day could invite volume litigation, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge, and small developers may struggle with the engineering demands of full deletion and access rights.

The savings clause expressly permits disclosure in compliance with a court order or legal process, so the bill does not keep this data out of the hands of parties who obtain it through legal proceedings; it governs companies' collecting and selling, not the courts.

Entities covered by HIPAA medical-privacy rules are excluded, so protections differ depending on whether the same information sits with a doctor's office or with an app, creating a gap at the seam between the two regimes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and specific: since the fall of nationwide abortion protections, a person's location and app data can reveal sensitive medical activity, and this bill would sharply limit who can collect and monetize it. The compliance and litigation costs are genuine but fall almost entirely on the companies profiting from the data trade. The design is aggressive but coherent; its weakest points are the HIPAA gap and the fact that it cannot reach data reached through court process.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.

narrative.text: Rep. Sara Jacobs introduced the bill in the House on June 11, 2025.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee with jurisdiction over consumer privacy.
The full action history shows no further action of any kind — no subcommittee referral, hearing, markup, or floor vote — since that referral.
The bill has 101 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat; no Republican has signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, data brokers and app companies are better off: with the bill stalled at referral, they continue collecting and selling reproductive and sexual health data under existing rules, and the public remains without the access, deletion, and lawsuit rights the bill would have created.

for.name: Rep. Sara Jacobs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the My Body, My Data Act of 2025 and recruited 101 cosponsors.

for.name: 101 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill; no Republican joined.

against.name: Rep. Brett Guthrie
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee that received the referral, has taken no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since June 2025.

sides.party_line_note: Support is entirely one-sided: all 101 cosponsors are Democrats, and with Republicans holding the House majority and the committee chairmanship, the bill has not advanced.

industries.note: Brokers currently buy and sell app and location data that can reveal visits to clinics or use of contraception; the bill would bar them from collecting or disclosing it and would let individuals sue for violations.

industries.industry: Reproductive and fertility app makers (period trackers, telehealth apps)
industries.note: They could keep offering their core services but would have to stop collecting, retaining, and sharing reproductive health data beyond what a user's request strictly requires, and would face deletion and access obligations. Users gain privacy at the expense of the companies' data monetization.
Targeted advertising built on reproductive health signals — searches, location pings near clinics, app activity — would be largely off-limits, cutting off a lucrative ad category.

industries.industry: Health care providers and HIPAA-covered entities
industries.note: They are expressly excluded from the bill and remain under HIPAA's existing privacy rules, so their practices are largely unchanged, though the exclusion leaves a gap between what a clinic may do with records and what an app may do with similar data.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and a Republican-led Energy and Commerce Committee that has taken no action in over six months, the bill is unlikely to receive a hearing or markup on its own. Its most realistic path forward would be provisions folded into a larger consumer-privacy package, if one materializes; on its own, it is likely to sit in committee until the Congress ends.
